analysis.one_liner: Bans the chemical bisphenol A in food and beverage containers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee in February 2011, it sat untouched until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell food in containers made with or releasing bisphenol A, a chemical widely used to line cans and hard plastics that can leach into food. It gave companies one-year renewable waivers if they could show no alternative was technically workable, required warning labels on any waived products, and directed the FDA to re-review other food-contact chemicals with attention to low-dose effects and vulnerable groups like infants and pregnant women.
analysis.who_benefits: Food consumers, especially babies, children, and pregnant women, who would no longer eat food that has been in contact with bisphenol A, a chemical that mimics estrogen and has been linked in animal studies to reproductive and developmental effects.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deems food adulterated if its container is made of bisphenol A or can release it into food, banning such containers from interstate commerce 180 days after enactment.

It lets companies that cannot yet replace bisphenol A get a one-year renewable waiver, but only if they prove no alternative is technologically feasible and submit a plan to remove it, and any waived product must carry a prominent warning label.

It requires the FDA to periodically re-review already-approved food-contact substances, weighing low-dose exposure and effects on infants, children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups, and to revoke authorizations for substances found unsafe.
It requires manufacturers of food-contact substances to certify that their chemicals cause no adverse effects at low doses and have not been shown to cause reproductive or developmental toxicity.

analysis.who_pays: Canned food and beverage makers, plastics and packaging manufacturers, and the chemical companies that produce bisphenol A would bear the cost of redesigning containers and switching to alternatives, some of which they argued were not yet available for every use.

drawbacks.text: Switching away from bisphenol A imposes real costs on food and packaging companies, which critics said would raise prices and that suitable alternatives, especially for hot-fill or acidic canned foods, were not proven for every use.

The bill also forces a standing re-review program for all previously approved food-contact substances, which is an ongoing regulatory burden on chemical and packaging suppliers even where products are ultimately found safe.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit falls on the whole population, and most heavily on infants, since bisphenol A lines most food and infant-formula cans and leaches into food. The costs fall on a narrow set of manufacturers, and the bill's waiver process is designed to phase out the chemical where alternatives exist while giving companies time where they do not. The main honest objection is scientific and regulatory: it restates FDA's authority over a contested chemical and adds a broad new review program, which industry said was unnecessary. On the other side, the FDA itself had already begun phasing out BPA in baby bottles and cups, suggesting reformulation was feasible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Edward Markey introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2011 on January 25, 2011, joined by three other House members as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and on February 9, 2011, referred it to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill attracted 34 additional cosponsors, all House Democrats, but no Republican signed on and no committee action followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food canners, packaging manufacturers, and bisphenol A producers kept selling BPA-lined containers unchanged for the rest of the Congress, since no ban or federal review schedule was put in place.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote, leaving it to die in the Health Subcommittee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support and no committee action, so the bill advanced entirely on one side of the aisle.

industries.industry: Canned and packaged food and beverage makers
industries.note: Nearly all metal food and beverage cans are lined with epoxy containing bisphenol A, which migrates into the food; the bill would force them to reformulate packaging or label products with a warning about it. Their cost of switching is directly the consumer's gain in reduced exposure.

industries.industry: Bisphenol A producers and epoxy resin makers
industries.note: The bill eliminates the market for one of the highest-volume industrial chemicals in food packaging, and the broader review program could remove other approved food-contact substances as well. Chemical makers argued BPA was safe at typical exposure levels.
Manufacturers that already make BPA-free bottles, jars, and can linings would gain customers as the entire market moved off BPA within 180 days, with waivers available only for proved exceptions.
